Obloquy has two closely connected meanings, and the full meaning of the word lives in both of them together.

The first meaning is harsh public verbal condemnation — when someone is spoken about very badly, attacked sharply in words, denounced openly, often by many people at once. Not quiet, private grumbling. Loud, forceful, public disapproval directed at a person.

The second meaning is the state of disgrace and damaged reputation that results from that kind of condemnation — when someone has been so thoroughly denounced that their name is stained, their honor is gone, and society looks down on them as a result.

Think of the two meanings as cause and effect: the fierce public condemnation (the act) and the lasting disgrace that it leaves behind (the result). When you use the word obloquy, you're almost always capturing both at once.

Three qualities define obloquy and make it a very specific kind of thing:

It is public. Obloquy is never a whisper in a corner. It happens out in the open — in newspapers, town squares, public discourse, or among communities. The exposure is part of what makes it so damaging.

It is strong. This is not mild criticism or a polite disagreement. Obloquy is fierce, heavy-handed condemnation — closer to denunciation than to disapproval.

It carries a moral charge. The person subjected to obloquy isn't merely disliked — they are seen as having done something shameful, dishonorable, or wrong. The condemnation isn't just "we don't agree with you." It's "you are a disgrace."

• After the general was exposed for abandoning his troops, he spent the rest of his life under a cloud of obloquy — shunned by former allies and condemned in every account of the war.
  • She had done nothing wrong, yet the obloquy heaped upon her by the press was so severe that she quietly left public life forever.
  • History sometimes redeems those who suffered obloquy in their own time — artists, scientists, and reformers who were mocked and condemned, only to be celebrated by later generations.
  • He accepted the obloquy without complaint, knowing that defending himself publicly would only make things worse.
How It Compares to Similar Words

Since obloquy sits in a neighborhood of words that all deal with condemnation and disgrace, it's worth understanding exactly where it stands.

Criticism is much milder and can be entirely private and constructive. Obloquy is always harsh, always public, and never constructive.

Insult is typically a single, sharp exchange between individuals. Obloquy is sustained, widespread, and social in nature.

Infamy focuses on the state of being widely known for something terrible — the famous-for-bad-reasons quality. Obloquy focuses more on the active process of being condemned in words, as well as the resulting disgrace.

Opprobrium is the word closest to obloquy — they are near-synonyms and often interchangeable. The faint distinction, if any, is that obloquy slightly emphasizes the spoken or written attacks directed at someone, while opprobrium slightly emphasizes the attitude of contempt and scorn that others hold. In practice, most careful writers treat them as equivalent.

Vilification refers specifically to the act of saying terrible things about someone to destroy their reputation. Obloquy covers both that act and the disgrace that results from it, giving it a slightly wider scope.
Register and Tone — When You'll Encounter This Word

Obloquy is a formal, literary word. You will almost never hear it in everyday conversation. You will encounter it in serious, careful writing — historical prose, literary fiction, formal essays, or high-register journalism. It tends to appear when the stakes are significant: political scandal, moral failure, public betrayal, or the ruin of a reputation.

When a writer reaches for obloquy instead of simply writing condemnation or disgrace, they are usually doing so deliberately — to give weight and gravity to what they're describing, and to capture both the verbal attacks and the resulting shame in a single, precise word.
If you had to boil it all down: obloquy is the fierce, public verbal condemnation of a person, and the lasting disgrace that such condemnation brings upon them.
